question.text: Which of the following CORRECTLY ranks asset classes from lowest to highest expected risk?

explanation.text: The Logic: The standard NISM risk hierarchy is cash, then debt, then equity. Cash and savings-style avenues are the lowest risk because principal is largely protected and returns are predictable. Debt instruments add credit risk (the issuer may default) and interest-rate risk (prices move inversely to rates), so they sit above cash. Equity has the highest expected risk because earnings, dividends and share prices can swing sharply in the short term, even though equity offers the highest long-term return potential. The Trap: 'Equity, then debt, then cash' reverses the order. 'Cash, then equity, then debt' wrongly places equity below debt. 'Debt, then cash, then equity' incorrectly puts debt below cash, ignoring debt's credit and interest-rate risk. Note: Rewrote the options as plain-English ordered lists (no greater-than/less-than symbols, which can be read ambiguously) and expanded the explanation so it covers debt and equity risk, not just cash.
